strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem: non-differentiable rewards in biomolecular design that cannot be handled by gradient-based methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (protein, DNA, small molecules) with consistent improvements over strong baselines (DDPO, DDPP, SFT) and competitive performance vs. DRAKES
Clear and well-motivated algorithmic framework with three intuitive phases: off-policy roll-in for exploration, value-guided roll-out for weighting, and forward KL distillation for stability
Theoretical insight connecting PPO objectives to reverse KL divergence (Theorem 1) with clear motivation for why forward KL may improve stability and reduce mode collapse

Excellent reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, comprehensive appendices, and good ablation studies on key design choices (lazy update interval K, roll-in mixture β)
Strong empirical improvements: meaningful gains on binding affinity (pLDDT 0.82 vs 0.55), DNA activity (8.28 vs 7.38), and molecular docking (9.4 vs 8.5)
Well-presented with clear figures, good motivation, and helpful visualizations of generated biomolecules with quantitative quality assessments
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: soft-optimal policies are standard in entropy-regularized MDPs, and value-weighted MLE is from prior RL work (Peters et al., 2010); the contribution is primarily a sensible combination of known techniques rather than a fundamental advance

Critical approximation (soft value function as point estimate v̂_{t-1} := r(x̂_0)) lacks rigorous justification for the fine-tuning setting; no analysis of approximation error, convergence implications, or empirical comparison to alternatives like Monte Carlo estimation
Absence of theoretical guarantees: no convergence rates, sample complexity bounds, or characterization of how approximations and lazy updates affect policy optimality

Soft-optimal policies defined w.r.t. pre-trained p^pre rather than the current fine-tuned policy; while lazy updates apply, the theoretical implications and potential optimality loss from this design choice are not discussed

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: different α values required per domain (1.0 vs. 6.0), non-monotonic performance in K (Table 8), and limited principled guidance for selecting hyperparameters on new tasks

Conflicting metric signals on DNA task: VIDD better on Pred-Activity and ATAC-Acc but worse on 3-mer Corr (0.162 vs. 0.398 for DDPO) without explanation; raises questions about which aspects actually improve

Stability claims not rigorously validated: no explicit metrics (gradient variance, loss landscape smoothness, run-to-run variance); only convergence curves provided; comparison with DDPO conflates on-policy vs. off-policy paradigms

Limited scope: all experiments on discrete diffusion for biomolecules; applicability to continuous diffusion and other domains unclear; no analysis of failure modes or settings where VIDD underperforms

Implementation details unclear: how exactly is exp(v_t(x_t)/α) incorporated into the roll-in distribution in practice; what happens when x̂_0 predictions are poor; robustness to denoising errors not analyzed
Missing computational analysis: no wall-clock time comparisons, sample efficiency evaluation (reward evaluations needed), or detailed cost comparison with inference-time methods like Best-of-N

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: fine-tuning diffusion models for non-differentiable rewards in biomolecular design, relevant to real scientific applications
Clear theoretical motivation comparing forward KL (VIDD) vs. reverse KL (PPO), with formal Theorem 1 showing the equivalence to mode-seeking behavior
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (protein, DNA, molecules) and diverse tasks with appropriate metrics for each domain
Consistent empirical improvements over DDPO and DDPP baselines across most tasks, with some notable gains (e.g., protein binding ipTM: 0.82 vs 0.79)
Well-structured presentation with detailed experimental setup, hyperparameter tables, and extensive appendices including ablations on lazy update interval K
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are from prior work—value-weighted MLE (Peters et al. 2010), soft-optimal policies (Uehara et al. 2025a), value approximation r(x̂₀) acknowledged as implicitly used in Wu et al., Li et al., and Chung et al. Main contribution is packaging these for diffusion fine-tuning, which feels incremental.

Critical unjustified value function approximation: Equation 4.2 replaces the conditional expectation E[exp(r(x₀)/α)|x̄ₜ₋₁] with a single deterministic point estimate r(x̂₀). This removes variance information and has no theoretical or empirical justification. No ablations comparing to Monte Carlo or regression-based estimates provided.

Marginal empirical improvements with overlapping error bars in many cases: SS-match (0.83±0.01 vs 0.81±0.02), DNA Pred-Activity (8.28±0.18 vs 7.38±0.11, ~5% gain), molecule docking (9.4±1.7 vs 8.5±1.3). Unclear if improvements are statistically significant or due to hyperparameter tuning.

Insufficient ablation studies: Missing ablations to isolate contributions of (1) off-policy nature, (2) forward KL minimization, (3) lazy updates, (4) value approximation quality. Only ablation on lazy update interval K provided, showing non-monotonic performance (suggesting hyperparameter sensitivity).

Hyperparameter fairness concerns: Different α values across tasks (1.0 to 6.0), different K schedules; unclear if baselines received equal hyperparameter tuning effort. No discussion of hyperparameter selection methodology or validation procedure.
Critical reproducibility failure: Missing code link on page 1 ('The source code is released at .' with no actual URL). This is unacceptable for a method paper at a top-tier venue.

Incomplete reward-diversity trade-off analysis: Tables 1-2 show diversity trade-offs (e.g., protein binding diversity 0.55 vs 0.53 for DDPO), but detailed analysis is relegated to appendix. Unclear if reported results represent final convergence or cherry-picked checkpoints.
Figure 4 inconsistency: Shows β_s=0.8 superior to β_s=1.0, but main results appear to use β_s=1.0 (not clearly stated). Suggests reported results may not be fully optimized.

Limited baseline comparisons: Missing PRDP (Deng et al. 2024, cited but not compared); DRAKES only on DNA task; no comparison to simpler offline RL baselines (CQL, AWAC, IQL applied to diffusion); Best-of-N treated as inference-time only.

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 is straightforward decomposition of PPO objective, providing useful intuition but not novel. No convergence analysis, theoretical guarantees, or analysis of approximation error from value function approximation.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical importance: addresses non-differentiable reward optimization in biomolecular design, a real limitation of existing methods
Strong theoretical motivation comparing PPO (reverse KL, on-policy) versus VIDD (forward KL, off-policy), with Theorem 1 providing clear justification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four distinct biomolecular domains (protein sequences, protein binding, DNA enhancers, small molecules) with consistent improvements
Multiple strong baselines including recent methods (DDPO, DDPP, DRAKES) with appropriate ablations on key hyperparameters (lazy update interval K, roll-in mixture β_s)
Pragmatic algorithmic design with efficient value function approximation that avoids training separate networks while maintaining computational efficiency
Excellent experimental methodology with extensive supplementary analyses, diversity-reward frontier visualization, and multiple naturalness metrics
Clear, well-organized presentation with strong motivation and logical flow from problem to solution to comprehensive validation
weaknesses: Value function approximation (v̂ = r(x̂_0)) replaces conditional expectation with point estimate but lacks rigorous justification or empirical validation; no sensitivity analysis or comparison to alternatives like Monte Carlo or regression-based approaches

Limited algorithmic novelty: value-weighted MLE (Peters et al. 2010), policy distillation (Czarnecki et al. 2019), and soft-optimal policies (recent work) are combined rather than novel; contribution is primarily in application to diffusion models
Insufficient theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity results, or formal justification for lazy update scheme; forward KL advantages mentioned but not deeply analyzed
Significant diversity-reward tradeoffs inadequately addressed: diversity drops from 0.91→0.52 (DNA) and 0.90→0.55 (protein binding) without clear guidance on when this is acceptable
Hyperparameter sensitivity: α varies substantially across tasks (1.0 vs 6.0) without principled guidance for selection in new domains; K and β_s also require tuning
Limited comparison with DRAKES: only evaluated on differentiable reward (DNA); comparison on non-differentiable or vice versa would strengthen claims

Missing efficiency analysis: no wall-clock time comparisons, sample efficiency (reward evaluations), or scalability assessment; unclear if training cost justifies improvements over inference-time methods
Generalization concerns: most experiments on discrete diffusion models; limited evidence for continuous diffusion beyond molecules; unclear transfer to other non-differentiable reward domains

strengths: Addresses important problem: non-differentiable reward functions in biomolecular design are practically relevant and not handled well by existing gradient-based or PPO-style methods
Comprehensive experimental validation across three domains (protein, DNA, molecules) with multiple tasks, appropriate baselines, and extensive ablations demonstrating consistent improvements

Practical algorithmic design: posterior mean approximation for value functions is computationally efficient, lazy updates prevent target drift, mixed roll-in balances exploration-exploitation, and off-policy formulation enables flexible data collection
Consistent empirical improvements: VIDD achieves best or competitive performance across diverse tasks (protein SS-match 0.83 vs 0.81 DDPO, DNA Pred-Activity 8.28 vs 7.38 DDPO)
Clear theoretical motivation: Theorem 1 provides useful intuition about forward KL (VIDD) vs reverse KL (PPO) and mode-seeking behavior
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, task descriptions, and extensive supplementary results enable verification
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution (value-weighted MLE, Eq. 5) comes from Peters et al. 2010; soft-optimal policies (Eq. 2) are temperature-scaled pre-trained policies; main innovations are engineering choices (lazy updates, mixed roll-in) rather than fundamental algorithmic advances

Weak theoretical justification for critical approximations: posterior mean approximation v̂_t(x) ≈ r(x̂_0(x)) lacks justification; why it outperforms Monte Carlo (only M=4 tested) and trained value networks is unexplained; creates approximation error in exponential weighting

Value function definition-practice mismatch: soft-optimal policies (Eq. 3) define values as expectations under pre-trained trajectories, but p^out diverges from p^pre during training with only lazy updates; this discrepancy deserves thorough analysis and its effect on convergence is unclear

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity without principled guidance: multiple critical hyperparameters (α, K, β_s) are task-dependent; K=5 optimal for DNA but suboptimal for ss-match (Table 16); no principled framework for new domains limits practical adoption

Reward-diversity trade-off unresolved: Table 2 shows protein binding achieves 0.82 ipTM but diversity drops to 0.55 vs 0.90 pre-trained; Table 1 shows ss-match diversity 0.52 vs 0.91 pre-trained; no multi-objective optimization framework provided

Critical dependence on reward signal quality: Appendix G shows performance halves with 10% reward noise; in practice, reward models have biases and noise but method offers no robustness mechanisms; limits real-world deployment

Incremental improvements with incomplete statistical analysis: many improvements marginal relative to error bars; DNA 3-mer correlation shows VIDD worse (0.162 vs 0.398 DDPO); molecule task metrics show tied or worse performance on secondary objectives (Table 12)
Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or characterization of when approximations are valid; Theorem 1 connection is qualitative rather than quantitative

Limited scope and generalization: tested only on specific pre-trained models (EvoDiff, GDSS); no experiments varying architecture, model size, or training procedures; all domains biomolecular—generalization unclear

Incomplete experimental comparisons: DNA task comparison with DRAKES somewhat unfair (designed for differentiable rewards); molecule task shows VIDD underperforms on fragment/scaffold similarity suggesting mode coverage issues despite higher reward

strengths: Addresses important practical problem of non-differentiable rewards in biomolecular design
Clear mathematical framework and rigorous formulation through entropy-regularized MDPs
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (proteins, DNA, molecules) with extensive ablations
Good motivation for why forward KL helps avoid mode collapse compared to reverse KL (Theorem 1)
Detailed reproducibility information including hyperparameters, hardware, and implementation details
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core components (value-weighted MLE, soft-optimal policies, lazy updates) are standard RL techniques; main contribution is application to diffusion models rather than methodological innovation

Crude value function approximation (v_t ≈ r(x̂_0)) replaces conditional expectation with single point estimate; justified only by computational cost, not approximation quality; Appendix F.2 shows Monte Carlo performs worse, suggesting fundamental limitations

Mixed empirical results with concerning patterns: significant diversity drops in binding tasks (28% reduction for IFNAR2); 3-mer correlation degrades substantially (0.162 vs 0.398); many improvements are modest and within error margins

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity: optimal K varies 5-50× across tasks; α varies 1-6×; β_s significantly affects performance; roll-in mixture critical but in appendix; suggests method requires extensive task-specific tuning
High sensitivity to reward noise: 10% Gaussian noise causes >60% performance degradation (Appendix G); real reward functions are noisy but robustness mechanisms absent

Unfair baseline comparisons: DNA evaluation includes DRAKES (gradient-based method with reward access) while emphasizing superior performance; missing comparisons to other recent off-policy/distillation methods in diffusion fine-tuning
Theoretical gaps: no convergence analysis, no approximation error analysis, no formal justification for forward KL diversity properties in diffusion setting, mode collapse claims are informal
Missing critical ablations: effect of value approximation quality itself, sensitivity of main results to roll-in mixture β_s (only in appendix), impact of value function parameterization choices

strengths: Addresses important practical problem: non-differentiable rewards in biomolecular design where gradient-based methods fail
Clear theoretical motivation connecting PPO to reverse KL divergence (Theorem 1) and providing principled rationale for forward KL + off-policy approach
Well-designed three-phase algorithm balancing exploration (off-policy roll-in), value guidance (soft-optimal policies), and stability (lazy updates)
Comprehensive experiments across diverse domains (protein, DNA, molecules) with consistent improvements over DDPO, DDPP, and other baselines
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, ablation studies on key hyperparameters (K, α, β_s) in appendices
Outperforms gradient-based method (DRAKES) on DNA despite handling non-differentiable rewards, demonstrating effectiveness of the approach
Clear presentation with effective figures (especially Figure 1 overview) and well-organized appendices
weaknesses: Soft value function approximation v̂_t(x) := r(x̂_0(x)) lacks rigorous justification; critical design choice treated informally with limited discussion of when approximation is valid or could fail
No convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or formal analysis of approximation error from posterior mean value estimates

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: K varies by task (Table 9: 8.28 at K=5 vs 7.06 at K=1), α and β_s substantially affect results, yet paper provides no principled method for selecting these on new problems
Poor robustness to noisy rewards: Tables 23-24 show 10% noise causes >50% performance degradation (0.91→0.47), concerning given inherent noise in real rewards from AlphaFold/docking

Diversity-reward tradeoff suggests potential mode collapse despite forward KL: DNA diversity drops from 0.91 to 0.52, protein binding from 0.90 to 0.55; 3-mer correlation drops dramatically, contradicting claim that forward KL prevents mode collapse
Missing computational cost analysis: no wall-clock time comparisons with baselines despite expensive reward functions (AlphaFold-Multimer 93M params), making practical deployment cost unclear
Some empirical improvements are modest and within error bars (e.g., protein SS-match 0.83±0.01 vs DDPO 0.81±0.02); no statistical significance testing; large standard errors in several metrics
Value function approximation not thoroughly explored: posterior mean performs worse than expected with Monte Carlo (Tables 21-22), counterintuitive result deserves deeper investigation
